pharm: A purified human plasma protein that provides the major contribution to plasma colloid oncotic pressure, drawing and holding fluid within the intravascular space and acting as a transport and buffering protein
quick: Individualised; e.g. 25 g (25%) initial for hypovolaemia; 8 g per L ascites removed
Use cautiously; risk of fluid overload - monitor
Used therapeutically (e.g. ascites/SBP); monitor for overload
Haemodynamics, fluid balance, signs of overload, serum albumin
summary: Human albumin is a plasma-derived colloid solution (commonly 5%, 20% or 25%) used to restore and maintain circulating blood volume and oncotic pressure. Indications include hypovolaemia/shock, large-volume paracentesis in cirrhotic ascites (about 8 g per litre of ascitic fluid removed), hypoalbuminaemia including burns, and selected other states. Dose is individualised to the patient's clinical condition and haemodynamics rather than a fixed amount. The 25% concentrated solution is hyperoncotic - it draws fluid into the circulation and can cause circulatory overload, so monitor volume status carefully, especially in cardiac and renal disease.
indications: Hypovolaemia (e.g. shock due to trauma or sepsis, surgical volume deficiency)
Prevention of central volume depletion after large-volume paracentesis in cirrhotic ascites
Hypoalbuminaemia including that associated with burns
Priming and fluid management in cardiopulmonary bypass

dosage.d: Initial 25 g (using 25% solution); for acute liver failure initial 12-25 g
dosage.n: Titrate to blood pressure, perfusion and volume status

dosage.d: About 8 g of albumin for every 1000 mL of ascitic fluid removed
Approximately 50-75 g, titrated to the deficit
dosage.t: Per clinical response and serum albumin
dosage.n: In burns, generally start after the first 24 hours

dosage.d: Individualised to body weight and clinical condition

admin: Inspect the solution - use only if clear and the container is undamaged; do not use if turbid or after the expiry date
May be given undiluted or diluted in 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% dextrose (do not dilute 25% in sterile water for injection - risk of haemolysis)
Adjust infusion rate to the indication and the patient's circulatory status; slow the rate if signs of overload appear
No ABO blood-group typing or cross-matching required
Use an administration set with an in-line filter where provided; discard partially used containers
moa: Albumin is the principal protein of human plasma and the major determinant of plasma colloid oncotic (osmotic) pressure. Infused albumin expands and maintains intravascular volume by retaining and attracting water across the capillary membrane; concentrated (20-25%) solutions are hyperoncotic and mobilise fluid from the interstitial space into the circulation. Albumin also binds and transports endogenous and exogenous substances (bilirubin, hormones, drugs, metals) and contributes to plasma buffering.

absolute: Severe anaemia or cardiac failure with normal or increased intravascular volume
Conditions in which hypervolaemia and its consequences (e.g. cardiac decompensation, pulmonary oedema) would be hazardous
relative: Hypertension, oesophageal varices, pulmonary oedema or bleeding diathesis
Conditions with risk of circulatory overload
monitor: Signs of circulatory overload and pulmonary oedema

preg: Albumin is a normal constituent of human plasma. No fetal risk is expected and it is considered safe to use in pregnancy when clinically indicated; nevertheless avoid unnecessary circulatory overload.
lact: Albumin is a normal plasma protein and is considered compatible with breastfeeding when clinically indicated.
renal: Use cautiously in renal impairment because the oncotic load can precipitate or worsen fluid overload and pulmonary oedema. Monitor volume status, electrolytes and renal function and adjust the rate and dose accordingly.
hepatic: Albumin is used therapeutically in liver disease (e.g. large-volume paracentesis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome). Monitor for circulatory overload and adjust dosing to clinical response.

major: No clinically significant pharmacologic drug interactions; main risk is volume/electrolyte effects when combined with other fluids
moderate: Do not mix in the same line with protein hydrolysates, amino-acid solutions or solutions containing alcohol (may cause protein precipitation)
minor: Plasma drug binding may shift transiently with large albumin loads
interactions.alcohol: Not applicable; avoid mixing with alcohol-containing solutions in the same line
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum albumin, haematocrit and electrolytes; large doses dilute coagulation factors

common: Usually well tolerated; mild reactions such as flushing, urticaria, fever or chills
serious: Dilutional coagulopathy or electrolyte disturbance with very large volumes
rare: Theoretical, extremely low residual risk of transmissible infectious agents from plasma source
emergency: Anaphylaxis (stop infusion, treat with epinephrine and supportive measures)

monitoring: Blood pressure, heart rate and central venous/haemodynamic status during infusion
Signs of circulatory overload (dyspnoea, raised JVP, pulmonary crackles)
counsel: This is a human plasma-derived product given by a drip; it carries an extremely low, theoretical risk of transmitting infection
Tell staff at once if you feel breathless, develop a rash, itching, flushing or chills during the infusion
The rate of the drip is adjusted to your condition and may be slowed if your body is holding too much fluid
Your blood pressure, breathing and fluid balance will be checked during treatment
pk: Plasma volume expansion is essentially immediate on infusion
Maximal oncotic effect of 25% solution within minutes to ~1 hour
Biological half-life of albumin approximately 18-20 days; intravascular distribution within hours
Volume effect of hyperoncotic albumin persists several hours, longer with normal capillary integrity
Store as labelled (commonly at or below 30 C or refrigerated per product); do not freeze; protect from light and use promptly once opened
pearls: Dose is individualised to haemodynamics, not a fixed amount - titrate to clinical response and serum albumin
25% (concentrated) albumin is hyperoncotic - watch for circulatory overload and pulmonary oedema
Standard regimen for large-volume paracentesis is about 8 g albumin per litre of ascites removed
Do not dilute 25% albumin in sterile water for injection (haemolysis risk) - use saline or dextrose
No blood group typing or cross-matching is needed
Discard if turbid and do not use partially used containers
missed: Albumin is administered by a healthcare professional according to clinical need, not on a fixed home schedule; there is no patient-managed missed dose.
overdose: Excessive or too-rapid infusion causes hypervolaemia and circulatory overload (hypertension, raised venous pressure, pulmonary oedema). Stop or slow the infusion immediately and manage with diuretics and supportive care, monitoring haemodynamics and respiratory status.
